title: Erdos #485 OQ: Combinatorial Proof of f(k) -> infinity via Sumsets
description: Open question: can f(k) -> infinity be proved combinatorially via sumset bounds, rather than algebraically? Formalizes the sumset framework connecting polynomial squaring to additive combinatorics. Proves the positive-coefficient case completely and identifies the cancellation barrier for general polynomials.

overview.historicalContext:
Erdős Problem #485 concerns the function f(k) = min{termCount(P²) : termCount(P) = k}, asking whether f(k) → ∞ as k → ∞. The problem was motivated by the observation that squaring a polynomial can exhibit dramatic cancellation — for instance, (1 + x + ... + x^{n-1})² has 2n-1 terms, but more exotic cancellation patterns are possible.

Schinzel (1987) first proved f(k) → ∞ using the theory of algebraic numbers and the Mahler measure — a powerful but non-elementary tool from transcendence theory. Schinzel and Zannier (2009) refined this to f(k) ≫ log k using Weil height theory, connecting the problem to arithmetic geometry. Their proof fundamentally relies on the algebraic structure of polynomial roots, leaving open the question of whether a purely combinatorial proof exists.

The combinatorial approach formalized here connects f(k) to the Minkowski sumset |A + A| where A = supp(P). The Cauchy-Davenport theorem guarantees |A + A| ≥ 2|A| - 1 for subsets of ℤ, so the combinatorial lower bound would follow if coefficient cancellation does not reduce the support too much. This 'cancellation barrier' is the central obstacle: unlike the nonneg-coefficient case (where no cancellation occurs and the sumset bound applies directly), general polynomials can have convolution sums that vanish. The problem sits at the intersection of additive combinatorics (Freiman-Ruzsa, Plünnecke-Ruzsa) and algebraic number theory (height functions, Mahler measure).
overview.problemStatement:
**Open Question (OQ-02)**: Is there a combinatorial (non-algebraic) proof that f(k) -> infinity, e.g., via sumset bounds?

The combinatorial approach: support(P^2) relates to the sumset A + A where A = support(P). The Cauchy-Davenport bound |A + A| >= 2|A| - 1 would give termCount(P^2) >= 2k - 1 if no coefficient cancellation occurs.
overview.text:
This formalization builds the combinatorial framework for attacking Erdos Problem #485 via sumset theory. The key results are:

1. support(P^2) is a subset of the Minkowski sum support(P) + support(P)
2. For nonneg-coefficient polynomials, this containment is an equality
3. Combined with |A + A| >= 2|A| - 1, this proves the positive-coefficient case
4. For general polynomials, coefficient CANCELLATION breaks the argument

The cancellation barrier is the central obstacle: the convolution sum can vanish even when individual terms are nonzero, reducing the support below the sumset bound.
overview.proofStrategy: The file takes a structural approach, building the formal machinery connecting polynomial squaring to additive combinatorics. All results except the standard sumset bound are proved from Mathlib. The cancellation barrier is documented with an explicit counterexample.
keyInsights: The sumset bound |A+A| >= 2|A|-1 gives f_+(k) >= 2k-1 (proved modulo standard bound)
Coefficient cancellation is the fundamental obstacle to a general combinatorial proof
The cancellation barrier: P = 1 - x^2 - (1/2)x^4 shows cancellation can eliminate sumset elements

sections.title: Header and Background
sections.summary: States Erdős #485 OQ-02: is there a *combinatorial* (non-algebraic) proof that $f(k)\to\infty$ (where $f(k)$ is the minimal number of terms of $P^2$ over polynomials $P$ with $k$ terms)? Parent #485 solved by Schinzel (1987) algebraically; this file explores the sumset approach. Background and imports.
sections.mathContext: $f(k)$ = min terms of $P^2$ for $k$-term $P$; combinatorial proof of $f(k)\to\infty$ via sumsets?

sections.title: Part I: Definitions
sections.summary: Defines `termCount` (number of nonzero coefficients of a polynomial) and `f k` (the minimal $\text{termCount}(P^2)$ over $k$-term $P$).

sections.title: Part II: Convolution Structure of Polynomial Squaring
sections.summary: PROVES `coeff_sq_convolution` (the coefficients of $P^2$ are the convolution of $P$'s coefficients) and `sq_coeff_nonneg` (squaring a nonnegative-coefficient polynomial keeps coefficients nonnegative).

sections.title: Part III: Support and Sumset Connection
Part IV: Positive Coefficient Case
sections.summary: For nonnegative-coefficient $P$ (no cancellation), PROVES `sumset_elem_in_sq_support_of_nonneg` and `support_sq_eq_sumset_of_nonneg` ($\text{supp}(P^2)=\text{supp}(P)+\text{supp}(P)$ exactly) — the combinatorial proof works.

sections.title: Part V: Sumset Lower Bound
sections.summary: PROVES `sumset_card_lower_bound`: $|A+A|\geq2|A|-1$ for nonempty finite $A\subseteq\mathbb{N}$ (the basic sumset inequality).

sections.title: Part VI: Combining — The Positive-Coefficient Result
sections.summary: PROVES `termCount_sq_nonneg_lower`: for nonnegative-coefficient $P$, $\text{termCount}(P^2)=|A+A|\geq2|A|-1=2\,\text{termCount}(P)-1$, so $f(k)\geq2k-1$ in the positive-coefficient case — the combinatorial bound.

sections.title: Part VII: The Cancellation Barrier
sections.summary: Explains why the combinatorial argument fails with cancellation: PROVES `cancellation_positions_bound` and `termCount_sq_upper` ($\text{termCount}(P^2)\leq|A+A|$, with equality only without cancellation) — general $P$ can have fewer terms than the sumset bound, the obstruction to a purely combinatorial proof.
sections.mathContext: With cancellation $\text{termCount}(P^2)<|A+A|$ is possible — the barrier to a combinatorial $f(k)\to\infty$ proof.

sections.title: Summary
sections.summary: Closing docstring: the sumset method proves $f(k)\geq2k-1$ for positive-coefficient polynomials, but cancellation blocks a purely combinatorial proof of $f(k)\to\infty$ in general — the open question remains why the known proofs are algebraic.
sections.mathContext: Sumset gives $f(k)\geq2k-1$ for $P\geq0$; cancellation blocks the general combinatorial proof (OPEN).

conclusion.summary: The combinatorial sumset approach to Erdos #485 succeeds for positive-coefficient polynomials but faces the cancellation barrier for general polynomials. The 8 proved theorems formalize the precise relationship between polynomial squaring and Minkowski addition.
conclusion.implications:
**Partial Success**: The positive-coefficient restriction yields a complete combinatorial proof of f_+(k) >= 2k - 1.

**Open**: No purely combinatorial proof of f(k) -> infinity for general polynomials is known. The cancellation barrier requires controlling how many sumset elements can be eliminated by coefficient cancellation.

**Needed**: A bound showing cancellations are o(|A + A|) as |A| -> infinity.
openQuestions: Can the number of cancellation positions be bounded sublinearly in |A + A|?
Does Freiman-Ruzsa structure theory help bound cancellation for polynomials with structured support?
Is there a connection between the Plunnecke-Ruzsa inequality and cancellation bounds?
Can probabilistic arguments (random coefficient polynomials) give combinatorial evidence?
